title: Resting from study
hook: even learning needs rest; mind and body both
tomorrow: the bar mitzvah's coming. so how does Eli keep learning after it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Psalm said God's teaching is sweeter than honey, and a fig tree always had one more fig. Today, the part of learning where you put the fork down.

Eleven tabs open, a highlighter running dry, and the words on the page starting to swim. Does the Torah ever say stop? It does, and in plain words. The book of Ecclesiastes, near its very end, says: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh." The Bible itself admits that reading the Bible can wear you out.
screen: `ELEVEN TABS, AND THE WORDS SWIM.` → `DOES THE TORAH EVER SAY STOP?` → `A WEARINESS OF THE FLESH.`

segments.voice: So the question for today: does learning need rest? The tradition's answer is yes, in mind and body. The Talmud remembers a teacher, Rabbah, who began his lessons with something funny, so his students would be cheered, and only then turned serious and began. Rest, built into the study itself. And the biggest rest is Shabbat. The Torah says God made the world in six days and on the seventh ceased and rested. Rest isn't a weakness; even the story of creation has it. A midrash, the Mekhilta, gives a line from Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya: the Sabbath is given to you, and you are not given to the Sabbath. Rest is a gift for people, not a test people serve. Here is a neighbor who says something close. In the Christian Gospel of Mark, Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Two traditions, each in its own book, saying rest exists for the person. And one honest difference. For Jews, Shabbat is the seventh day, from Friday's sundown into Saturday night, with its own laws of rest, and for some it's a day when study becomes a pleasure, not a task. A friend's Lutheran church may keep Sunday as its day of worship instead, for its own reasons. Same need for rest. Different day, different shape.
screen: `DOES LEARNING NEED REST?` · `RABBAH STARTS WITH A JOKE.` · `THE SABBATH IS GIVEN TO YOU.` · `A NEIGHBOR: MADE FOR MAN.` · then, large: `REST FROM STUDY TOO.`

segments.voice: Close whatever you're reading and set it aside. Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up, and let your shoulders drop. For the length of the sit, do nothing useful at all, and let that be enough.
screen: `CLOSE IT. SET IT ASIDE.` · `HANDS OPEN IN YOUR LAP.` · `NOTHING USEFUL AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Resting from study: the pause that keeps learning alive. Ecclesiastes says much study wearies the body; Shabbat says rest is a gift.
Carry this: rest from study too, because the Sabbath was given to you. See you after the break.

howItsDone: Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall as a day of rest, and for some it is a day for unhurried study and conversation rather than work.
